In this rich, scholarly, and superbly illustrated book, Fletcher explores how fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Italy produced various kinds of innovative firearms, transforming war, politics, and society. The constant battles between Italian city-states encouraged local gun manufacturers to continually produce better weapons. But because these companies could not rely solely on their own governments for sales, they looked to export their wares to foreign states—and even to civilian buyers. As gunmakers made and shipped more weapons, these arms ceased to be the preserve of the aristocracy. Instead, they came into the hands of ordinary people, helping them challenge the existing social order. Fletcher, a historian, also shows that modern debates about gun control were present from the start. The efforts of states to restrict firearm access came up against demands for self-defense, manufacturer opposition, and the inability of those states to enforce their own rules.
